evidence: Plaut. Aul. 133: eō nunc ego sēcrētō tēd hūc forās sēdūxī
Cic. Att. 5.21.12 (Lewis & Short): mē rūrsus sēdūcit
terms.comment: Latin puts “aside” in the prefix sē-, “apart”: sēdūcere, to lead aside; sēvocāre, to call aside; sēcēdere, to step aside. Classically it never means “seduce”: that sense, to lead astray, is Christian Latin (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Caes. B.G. 5.6 (Lewis & Short): sēvocāre singulōs hortārīque coepit
terms.comment: A favourite word of Cicero’s (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Plaut. Curc. 2.3.2 (Lewis & Short): abīte et dē viā sēcēdite
terms.comment: Sēcēde hūc, step over here (for a private word), is the comic formula; so concēde hūc (Plaut. Men. 158).
Apart from the others: Plautus has sēdūxit sōlum sorsum ab aedibus (As. 362), with the old short form. For a word in private, sēcrētō.

phrases.latin: Sēcēde hūc. nam sunt quae ex tē sōlō scītārī volō.
phrases.english: Step aside over here: there are things I want to ask you alone.

phrases.latin: eō nunc ego sēcrētō tēd hūc forās sēdūxī, ut tuam rem ego tēcum hīc loquerer familiārem.
phrases.english: That’s why I’ve taken you aside out here privately, to talk with you about your family affairs.
